content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides a manually curated dataset for domain generalization experiments designed around graphical developments of a videogame series spanning a transition from 2D to 3D graphics. Researchers collected video data from the games, constructed a four class classification problem from those data, and treat each game as a unique domain. The paper evaluates this dataset for difficulty as a classification problem (easy), as a single or multi-domain generalization problem (hard), and as auxiliary data for other domain generalization tasks (modestly useful). An additional analysis compares the new domain to two existing tasks in terms of JPEG compression, finding the three tasks differ in levels of compression ratios and the closeness of these ratios among the domains in each dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

1. Novel source for domain generalization datasets. The approach in the paper could easily generalize to more classes, other games, and the general notion of using increasing visual fidelity in simulations for datasets.


## Weaknesses

1. It is not clear what the JPEG analysis explains. The smoothness of domain changes seems to be a difference among the domains examined, but there is no quantitative assessment of how that correlates with domain generalization difficulty or benefits from using the domains as additional training data. While an interesting hypothesis, no results directly test a concrete claim around the compression ratios. This idea would be bolstered by pinning down and performing a hypothesis test. More details on one case below.
2. Modest results. The experiments clearly demonstrate the generalization task is hard in the Mario dataset. The augmentation results show only a very modest benefit (~0.1-0.2 percentage points for ERM, though 1.4PP for SWAD to bring it to match the ERM ceiling performance) and do not claim SOTA level benefit. The paper would strengthen the claims for the Mario dataset by showing that it provides superior benefits to other datasets as an augmentation technique.
3. I have some specific concerns around the classes in the Mario dataset detailed below, specifically around how comparable some of the classes are. It would help to provide metrics that show that each class is the "same" (and the source for the original choice) in relevant empirical dimensions. This comes up as many datasets pick classes like animals or objects where it is easy to define a given entity as that object. Defining a scene as "castle" is more ambiguous (for example, when considering the spiral floating in open space for "Wii").


## Feedback & Questions
- Table 7: The table would benefit from a baseline augmentation for comparison. What happens if you add the same number of samples from VLCS to ImageNet1K as added in the "ImageNet1K + Mario" case? This will back the claim that the particular structure of the Mario dataset is beneficial as opposed to the claim that the quantity of data is what provides the benefit. The comparison would also provide additional evidence around whether JPEG compression can be used to measure domain similarity and the proposed smoother scaling hypothesis.
- The out of domain transfer experiments report results after resizing and gray scaling. Were those transformations (and training budget, hyperparameters, &c.) applied to produce the results in Table 2? This would help comparison by providing Table 2 as a baseline that establishes how hard the "in-domain" task is. If the two use different training regimes we cannot make that comparison. Alternatively, adding that baseline to set the upper bound on performance would help contextualize the results reported in Tables 5 & 6.
- How should we interpret the results from the MSDG experiments compared to the baseline algorithm performance and JPEG compression? The MSDG results in Table 5 suggest the Mario domain transfer task is hard. Table 2 suggests the domains themselves are individually easy. The JPEG compression results show a smaller range of compression rates, interpreted in the text as a smoother domain shift. It is not clear what to make of these results together. If the target task is easy (Table 2) the MSDG transfer should depend on how similar the domains are. If JPEG compression indicates domain similarity (at least for classification) (Table 4), then the Mario domains are similar. But the transfer task results show poor performance for the baseline algorithms (Table 5 & 6).
- Figure 1: The "Underground" and "Castle" classes seem very different in the N64 and Wii domains, relative to the "Overworld" and "Aquatic") classes. This leads me to wonder how much the transfer challenge is dominated by the difficulty of transfer on these classes. It would help to provide (in the Appendix) a confusion matrix, particularly for some of the transfer tasks. It would also help to provide a link to the dataset and definitions for which levels were used for each of the classes and domains. This would support reproducibility and augmentation of the dataset.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity: The text is readable and straightforward to follow.
- Quality: The experiments are hard to compare and it is not clear how to combine the results presented into an understanding of the dataset.
- Originality: Using a game series across implementations is a novel idea to introduce when thinking about the concept of "domains".
- Reproducibility: The dataset will presumably be provided in the final version. Relevant details on its construction are absent (ex: which levels are used for which classes).
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall the paper introduces two main ideas: using graphical changes in a game series (with shared content) for a domain generalization task and analyzing domain structure in terms of JPEG compression ratios. The new domain generalization dataset is hard, though not in ways that seem novel or extreme compared to similar datasets. The results do not show what is specific to the novelty of using a game series that makes this task a useful benchmark for algorithm performance or a powerful tool for data augmentation compared to alternatives. This leaves the claim primarily one that highlights a new potential source for datasets in domain generalization with ambiguous potential.

JPEG compression is one way to examine dataset structure and the paper shows there may be differences among the three datasets compared. I believe this will extend to other datasets and may prove to be a useful metric (alongside metrics based in the vast array of human perception models) for analyzing domain generalization datasets. The results do not provide any quantitative evidence that JPEG compression helps explain how hard domain generalization is or how useful a dataset is for augmenting training in domain generalization. The idea is promising, but results are not yet present.

Taken together the paper advances interesting ideas that can be useful additions if they show clearer empirical benefits.

content.details_of_ethics_concerns:
The dataset is from user-uploaded videos of playing copyrighted games. I am not deeply familiar with the legal issues here, but at least three potential problems come to mind:
1. Rights to obtain and share the data from Youtube and Twitch.tv
2. Rights & permissions granted to use the gameplay data from players.
3. Legal rights & permissions to distribute gameplay screenshots from proprietary games.

Many of these may be non-issues for being public in some form, but I do not know well. Nintendo (owner of the Mario franchise and these games) is notorious for being strict about taking down gameplay videos from streaming in the past.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new dataset for domain generalization (DG).  The dataset is divided into four domains, each of which corresponds to a different generation console, and the labels are one of four different Mario environments.  The authors benchmark various DG algorithms on their dataset and discuss a heuristic metric for measuring domain shift.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

**Problem setting.**  DG is an important and relevant problem in applications.  Many algorithms and datasets have been proposed for this setting.  However, there has not yet been significant progress in improving OOD robustness.  And therefore, any algorithm/dataset that can advance our understanding of the problem has potentially high impact.

## Weaknesses

**Motivation.**  This paper proposes a new dataset.  As such, it is essential that the authors motivate precisely why there is a need for a new dataset in this field.  It's worth noting that in recent times, there have been many datasets proposed for this setting, including those in the DomainBed and WILDS families.  Therefore, the question here is: What's new?  And why is there need for this benchmark?

Having read the paper, I'm not sure what the answer is to either of the above questions.  I welcome the authors thoughts in the discussion period regarding these questions, because I'm more or less at a loss.  The motivation seems to be that there is a "lack of understanding of the magnitude of domain shift" and that this dataset addresses this gap.  But it's unclear how this dataset gets us closer to understanding how to measure domain shift.  To illustrate this, consider the following passage:

> "We do not have a quantitative measure to implicate whether the domain shift gap from photos to sketches is many times larger than the gap from photos to paintings."

I agree with this statement.  But could the same criticism not be applied to this new Mario dataset?  As far as I have understood, in the new dataset, there is no metric that tells us how far apart the Wii is from the NES console.  Yes, these consoles come from different eras with different resolutions and technologies, but beyond that, one would be hard-pressed to come up with a metric -- a mathematical distance function -- which captures the distance between these domains.  

And so to summarize, given that the novelty in this paper is almost solely involved in convincing the reader that this dataset offers something new to the community, I find the motivation to be insufficient in two ways.  First, the dataset doesn't seem to satisfy the authors' own criteria regarding why this dataset is needed.  And second, the motivation used in the first place -- which is that we don't know how to measure domain shift -- also seems shaky, as it is hard to see how the introduction of a dataset of this form could actually resolve this problem.

**Relationship to past work.**  Consider the following passage:

> "Previous datasets for image Domain Generalization ignore such transitional graphic quality improvements, oftentimes addressing solely the overall domain shift such as synthetic versus photorealistic. Our dataset features a much fine-grained visual domain shift design that challenges the robustness of current high performing DG approaches."

I may be missing something, but it's unclear to me how this dataset offers a more "fine-grained" notion of shift.  What makes this kind of shift more interpretable than the shifts in PACS or VLCS?  It seems that the proposed dataset actually has relatively similar characteristics -- it is an image dataset with four domains, each of which have distinct visual features.  This could easily describe SuperMario Domains or PACS.

So again I emphasize the point: What should the reader take away from this paper in terms of novelty?  In what specific use-cases could this dataset improve our understanding of domain generalization?

**JPEG compression.**  The authors note that:

> "However, previous DG datasets adopted as benchmarks on this task often resort to measuring the domain shift by feature space distances using metrics such as KL-Divergence or t-SNE (Li et al., 2017). Such metrics do not provide quantified magnitude of domain shift in between the domains and does not show potential domain overlaps. Instead, it only shows that the domains are separable somehow, reflected in the performance difference across the domains."

They then propose JPEG compression as a metric for determining the differences between domains.  However, from my understanding, it seems as if this metric falls into the same trap as the metrics mentioned above.  In particular, perhaps the authors could elaborate on why JPEG compression rates provide a "quantified magnitude of domain shift" in a significantly better way than KL divergence or t-SNE.  I agree with the authors that the latter two metrics do not provide a meaningful measure.  However, in order to convince the reader that JPEG compression is better, the authors should construct an argument to make their case for JPEG that is not specific to this particular dataset.  I suppose it seems somewhat reasonable that images from older consoles are more compressible than later consoles.  However, looking beyond this dataset, it's unclear why this is a good measure of domain shift.  The results on PACS and VLCS show different numbers, but there doesn't seem to be an attempt to validate whether or not lower/higher numbers correspond to easier/harder shifts to generalize to.

The question to keep in mind here is: Does this metric advance our understanding of domain generalization?  And ultimately, while one can make a heuristic argument as to why this metric makes sense for this particular benchmark, it's unclear what the impact of this would be.  If, in a hypothetical scenario, the authors had an *explicit* expression for the amount of domain shift in this dataset, it may be more impactful.  However, as JPEG compression is just a heuristic that seems to correlate with the console version, I think this falls short of the bar for an impactful contribution.

**Marginal improvements on PACS.**  The benefits of pre-training on PACS seem to be relatively marginal.  Table 7 shows that we can get 1 or 2 percentage points of improvement.  I'm not sure what the impact of this result is.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity and quality.**  This paper is clearly written for the most part.  The grammar is shaky at times, but it's one of the better-written papers in my batch.

**Novelty.**  I'm not sure there are any especially novel aspects of this work.  

**Reproducibility.**  Will this dataset be made public?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while this dataset aims to improve our understanding of DG, I believe that the contribution is relatively marginal.  It's not clear to me how this dataset advances our understanding of the problem, and why it offers new insights over existing benchmarks.  The empirical results also do not shed new light on the problem, and the JPEG compression metric seems (a) only applicable to this benchmark and (b) relatively heuristic.  Therefore, while I like the direction of this paper, I feel that it is not ready for publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new multi-domain Domain Generalization (DG) dataset, SuperMarioDomains, which is inspired by evolving technology of video game graphics. The dataset images come from 4 versions of Super Mario games and contains both 2D and 3D graphics. The author did the following experiments to evaluate the datasets quality: 
1) in the compression metric for domain style shift, the Mario dataset has the second highest deviations and provides a smoother domain shift with smaller gaps in between the domains.  
2) In Single-Source Domain and Multi-Source Domain Generation Experiments, the author evaluated the results of many kinds of Domain Generation methods. And the result shows that there is no method performs significantly better.
3) In out of domain classification, the experiment shows that with Mario dataset during the pretrain, the SOTA methods have better results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The paper proposes a new DG dataset, which comes from the Mario games, the image source is novel enough.
+ The experiments show that the Mario dataset provides new benchmarks for domain generation tasks.
+ With the Mario dataset, we can find that there is no best method for Mario Domain Generation.
+ Mario dataset help improve out of domain classification.

Weaknesses:
- The compression metric shows that PACS has higher deviations because its sketch domain. Could the author create some Mario dataset that is similar with the PACS Sketch domain and test the results? Since the Mario dataset comes from man-made image, I think it is easy to get Sketch like Mario datasets. 
- In Table 7, the author evaluated the out of domain classification and the results shows that with Mario datasets the SOTA methods have better results, However, I consider other DG dataset performance, for example VLCS.
- The dataset needs to be tested with more methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is good in clarity, quality and novelty. Since the main contribution is the new dataset, there is no problem in reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper gives a news dataset which comes from Mario game, and the paper has enough experiments to evaluate the datasets. However, the dataset needs to be test with more works.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a new dataset collected from the game SuperMario released in different times for domain generalization (DG). It benchmarks existing DG algorithms using the proposed dataset and shows the discrepancy between different domains quantitatively. Moreover, it shows using the proposed dataset for pretraining could lead to better classification performance on PACS benchmark.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ A new dataset constructed from game

I do not fully understand the motivation of using SuperMario game for the data source. Is it indicating that other games could also serve as the source? I feel building the motivation of building or using those synthetic data is considered for real data use case. For example, CYNTHIA is a synthetic city game data with a lot labels, which can be leveraged to research and explore how to benefit real city scenes like those data in Cityscape, to reduce the domain gap and encourage better model generalization. However, for SuperMario, it is hard for me to understand why choosing this game as a source. Is it just because that it has four different hardware versions so that it could be used for classification? It is not like sketches or painting which contain a lot of objects in our daily life but just in a different form. The four defined scene classes look not quite applicable to real use cases.

For the exp on PACS, in addition to adding data, have authors try some existing color or style transfer method to transfer the style of SuperMario to sketch or photos, which is essentially a type of data augmentation? This will further demonstrate whether such a dataset is necessary or just some low-level characteristics will help improve the performance.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is organized clearly. Reproducibility is up to the release of the proposed dataset. Game data is less explored before so the originality is there but I'm not sure about the motivation.
content.summary_of_the_review: My biggest concern lie in the motivation of using this specific game data. It is too far from our daily life.
